title: 第五章　阶级敌人的秘密：斯捷潘·波德卢布内
originalTitle: 5　Secrets of a Class Enemy: Stepan Podlubny

children: 斯大林的工业化运动将数以百万计的人从广袤苏联土地上的村庄席卷到城市，以及第一个五年计划期间不断扩张的建设工地。他们成了将俄罗斯重塑为社会主义国家工程中不可或缺的劳动力。在协助催生新世界的同时，这些农民工也需要重塑自我。斯大林的规划者将新兴的工业景观构想为一个扩展的“灵魂工厂”。农民们作为“旧的人类材料”来到这里，背负着传统、迷信和狭隘利己主义的重负。在集体劳动和随之而来的政治教育的共同影响下，他们要将自己重塑为社会主义公民。工厂管理人员热切地招募那些为了寻求更美好未来，或者仅仅是为了逃离因阶级斗争而变得生活无法忍受的村庄而来的农民工。

Stalin’s industrialization campaign swept millions of people from the villages of the vast Soviet land into the cities and onto the sprawling construction sites of the First Five-Year Plan. They formed an indispensable workforce for the project of remaking Russia into a socialist state. While helping bring the new world into being, these peasant-workers also were to remake themselves. Stalinist planners conceived of the emerging industrial landscape as an extended factory of the soul. The peasants arrived there as “old human material,” weighed down by the forces of tradition, superstition, and narrow egoism. Under the combined influence of collective labor and attendant political education they were to remold themselves into socialist citizens. Factory managers avidly recruited peasant laborers who arrived in search of a better future, or merely to escape villages where class war had made their lives unbearable.

然而，党内官员却感到警惕。他们怀疑数十名富农（kulaks）——农村剥削资产阶级的成员——在难以控制的农村向城市的人流中潜伏了起来。人们担心这些富农披上好工人的伪装来欺骗政权，但在核心上却抵制社会主义再教育的精神，并阴谋推翻苏维埃政权。用当时的语言来说，他们是“披着羊皮的狼”。对付他们唯一有效的方法就是撕下虚假的外衣，裸露其敌对的本质。检查工人的证件是识别伪装敌人的方法之一。然而，证件可以伪造。归根结底，只有布尔什维克的警惕，对个人行为和思想的不断试探，才能辨别谁经得住考验，可以进入无阶级的社会主义社会。

Party officials, however, were alarmed. They suspected that scores of kulaks—members of the exploiting rural bourgeoisie—had gone into hiding amid the uncontrollable rural-to-urban flow. It was feared that these kulaks assumed the guise of good workers to deceive the regime, but at their core resisted the spirit of socialist re-education and plotted to bring down Soviet power. They were, in the language of the times, “wolves in sheep’s clothing.” The only effective way to deal with them was to tear off the false cover and bare their hostile essence. To check workers’ documents was one way of identifying enemies in disguise. Yet documents could be forged. Ultimately only Bolshevik vigilance, the constant probing into individuals’ deeds and thoughts, could tell who did and who did not pass the litmus test for acceptance into the classless socialist society.

斯捷潘·波德卢布内就是这样一头伪装的狼。作为一个富农的儿子，他在集体化期间逃离了他的乌克兰村庄并定居在莫斯科，伪装成工人阶级出身。波德卢布内从1931年到1939年一直记日记，然后从1941年直到生命尽头。在日记中，他记录了在猎巫式搜捕和不断揭露阶级敌人的氛围下，为了融入新环境而付出的艰辛努力。但波德卢布内的日记也清楚地表明，他看待自己的新生活不仅仅是一个掩饰的问题，而且是一个实现自我彻底重构的机会，其目标是成为一名真正的社会主义社会成员。尽管是布尔什维克镇压的受害者，他却将自己重塑为革命自我改变的主体。他所面对的核心问题是他内心新旧力量之间的紧张关系。他表达了很大的希望：布尔什维克意识形态中那种整合的一面——即规定只要真诚地、全身心地参与建设，任何人都可以加入社会主义社会——能适用于他的情况。与此同时，他始终意识到该政权的迫害热忱，以及他可能被不可磨灭地打上敌人烙印的危险。两个矛盾的问题标志着他在整个1930年代的生活：他能否成功掩盖自己的异己身份并逃过苏维埃政权的惩罚性注视？以及，从长远来看，狼能否变成羊？

Stepan Podlubny was one such wolf in disguise. The son of a kulak, he fled his Ukrainian village during collectivization and settled in Moscow, pretending to be of working-class background. Podlubny kept a diary from 1931 until 1939, then from 1941 to the end of his life. In it he documented his strenuous efforts to blend in with his new environment in a climate of witch hunt and unremitting exposure of class enemies. But Podlubny’s diary also makes clear that he looked upon his new life not merely as a matter of dissimulation but as a chance to achieve a total reconstruction of his self, with the goal of becoming a genuine member of socialist society. Though a victim of Bolshevik re-pression, he remade himself into an agent of revolutionary self-change. The central problem he grappled with was the tension between the forces of the old and the new within him. He expressed much hope that the integrative side of Bolshevik ideology, which stipulated that anyone could join socialist society if he partook in its construction sincerely and wholeheartedly, would apply to his case. At the same time he remained aware of the regime’s persecutory zeal and the danger that he might be indelibly stamped as an enemy. Two contradictory questions marked his life throughout the 1930s: Could he successfully mask his alien identity and escape the punitive gaze of the Soviet regime? And, in the longer term, could the wolf turn into a sheep?

波德卢布内1914年出生在乌克兰文尼察区的一个农户家庭。作为独子，他在一个几代人依靠农业和贸易生活并积累了可观财富的家庭中长大。当斯捷潘的祖父叶夫多基姆去世时，他的六个儿子每人继承了15俄亩土地，其中大部分在革命过程中丧失了。斯捷潘的父亲菲利普·叶夫多基莫维奇在1914年被征召入伍并很快被奥地利人俘虏，1918年回国后，他的土地除了4俄亩以外全部被剥夺。尽管如此，波德卢布内一家在1920年代的苏维埃村庄仍被视为富农阶级的农民剥削者。斯捷潘在家说乌克兰语，并在一家乌克兰七年制学校上学，在那里俄语被作为外语教学。他学习有困难，因为他父亲每年春天都让他停课去地里干活。在每年的暑假里，家里都会雇一名导师，给斯捷潘补上他错过的课程。

Podlubny was born in 1914 into a peasant household in the Vinnitsa district of Ukraine. An only child, he grew up in a family that for generations had lived from agriculture and trade and had acquired considerable wealth. When Stepan’s grandfather Evdokim died, each of his six sons inherited fifteen desiatinas of land, most of which was lost in the course of the revolution. Stepan’s father, Filip Evdokimovich, who was drafted as a soldier in 1914 and soon captured by the Austrians, was stripped of all but four desiatinas of his landholdings after his return home in 1918. Nevertheless, the Podlubnys were regarded in the Soviet village of the 1920s as members of the kulak class of peasant exploiters. Stepan spoke Ukrainian at home and attended a Ukrainian seven-year school in which Russian was taught as a foreign language. He had difficulty learning because his father took him out of school every spring to work in the fields. During the annual summer vacation the family hired a tutor who taught Stepan the parts of the syllabus he had missed.

随着1920年代后期激进工业化运动的启动，官方对富农的政策变得日益敌对。1929年春天，政府引入了“自我征税”原则，将确定每个当地家庭欠税粮食数量的权力移交给当地苏维埃。村苏维埃将绝大部分粮食税强加在富农户身上，从而迫使他们陷入贫困。未能完成配额的家庭会被课以重罚。在大多数情况下，这种恶性循环以没收整个农场告终。这就是波德卢布内一家的命运。文尼察别廖佐夫卡村苏维埃于1929年10月出具的一份证明指出，菲利普·波德卢布内的财产包括一所房子、一个谷仓和4俄亩农田。该证明进一步宣布，波德卢布内不拥有任何农具，并已在前一个春天将其全部库存作为交粮义务的一部分移交给了村苏维埃。

1929至1930年的冬天，波德卢布内一家的财产被彻底没收。由于未能履行对国家的义务，菲利普·波德卢布内被捕并被驱逐到阿尔汉格尔斯克，接受为期三年的行政流放。菲利普的妻子叶夫罗西尼娅·丹尼洛夫娜和斯捷潘暂时幸免，但他们不得不离开家，家被移交给了一个“无产阶级农民”家庭，而他们自己则定居在村边一个废弃的小屋里。在一篇被广泛刊登的文章中，斯大林重申了共产主义国家的目标：“作为一个阶级消灭富农”，并使苏维埃社会摆脱其“最野蛮、最粗鲁、最残暴的剥削者”，即那些以劳动人民为代价致富的“蜘蛛”、“吸血鬼”和“吸血虫”。

1930年春天，斯捷潘的母亲离开了别廖佐夫卡村，去阿尔汉格尔斯克与丈夫团聚，她使用了一个与她同名但未被归类为富农的堂表亲的个人证件。斯捷潘留下完成他最后一年的学业。作为富农的儿子，法律上可以禁止他上学，但学校校长允许他读完这一年。校长秘密地给他发了毕业成绩单，但敦促他尽快离开村子。事实上，正如斯捷潘多年后得知的，村里的共青团积极分子一直在准备逮捕他。在朋友的支持下，斯捷潘获得了去阿尔汉格尔斯克的火车票。在火车上，警察没收了他所有的证件，他的旅程似乎结束了。但多亏了一连串幸运的情况，他最终到达了阿尔汉格尔斯克并找到了父母。

With the launching of the radical industrialization campaign in the late 1920s, official policies toward kulaks turned increasingly hostile. In the spring of 1929 the government introduced the principle of “self-taxation,” transferring to local soviets the power to determine the amount of grain each local household owed in taxes. The village soviets imposed the overwhelming part of the grain tax on kulak households, thereby forcing them into destitution. Households that did not fulfil their quotas were heavily fined. In most cases, this vicious circle ended in the confiscation of the entire farm. This was the fate of the Podlubny family. A certificate issued by the Beryozovka village soviet, dated October 1929, stated that Filip Podlubny’s property included a house, a barn, and four desiatinas of farm land. The certificate further declared that Podlubny did not own any farm tools and had transferred his entire inventory to the village soviet in the preceding spring as part of his grain delivery obligations.

In the winter of 1929–30 the Podlubnys’ property was completely expropriated. Because of his failure to fulfill his obligations to the state, Filip Podlubny was arrested and deported to Arkhangelsk for a three-year sentence of administrative exile. Filip’s wife, Yefrosinia Danilovna, and Stepan were spared for the time being, but they had to leave their home, which was handed over to a family of “proletarian peasants,” and settle in an abandoned hut on the edge of the village. In a widely published article, Stalin reiterated the goal of the Communist state: to “liquidate the kulaks as a class” and free Soviet society of its “most beastly, rawest, and most brutal exploiters,” the “spiders,” “vampires,” and “bloodsuckers” who had enriched themselves at the cost of the laboring people.

In the spring of 1930 Stepan’s mother left the village of Beryozovka and joined her husband in Arkhangelsk, using the personal documents of a cousin who shared her first name but was not classified as a kulak. Stepan remained behind to complete his final year at school. As the son of a kulak, he could be legally barred from attending school, but the school director allowed him to finish the year. The director secretly issued him a graduation transcript, but urged him to leave the village as quickly as possible. Indeed, as Stepan learned years later, Komsomol activists in the village had been preparing to have him arrested. With the support of friends, Stepan obtained a train ticket to Archangelsk. On the train the police confiscated all his documents, and his journey seemed over. But thanks to a string of lucky circumstances, he ultimately reached Archangelsk and found his parents.

在接下来的1930至1931年冬天，斯捷潘和母亲离开了阿尔汉格尔斯克，打算回到家乡。此时斯捷潘也有了显示他是工人出身的伪造证件。在莫斯科的基辅火车站，他们遇到了乌克兰同乡农民，他们报告了对富农家庭成员和亲属的逮捕，并敦促他们不要再继续走下去。母子俩留在莫斯科寻找工作。几个月内，两人都找到了稳定的工作，斯捷潘的母亲当了门卫，斯捷潘则在《真理报》印刷厂的工厂学校当学徒。他们住在莫斯科市中心，住在母亲工作的建筑物的一个潮湿的地下室房间里。命运弄人，这两个伪装的阶级异己的新家竟然位于“红无产阶级街”。

In the following winter, 1930–31, Stepan and his mother left Archangelsk, intending to return to their home village. By now Stepan, too, had forged documents showing him to be of worker origins. At the Kievskaya train station in Moscow they encountered fellow Ukrainian peasants, who reported arrests of kulaks’ family members and dependents and urged them not to travel any further. Mother and son remained in Moscow and looked for work. Within a few months both found steady employment, Stepan’s mother as a janitor, and Stepan as an apprentice in the factory school of the Pravda printing plant. They lived in central Moscow, in a humid basement room of the building in which the mother worked. It was an ironic twist of fate that the new home of these two class aliens in disguise was located on Red Proletarian Street.

波德卢布内在他加入《真理报》之前不久就开始在日记本上写作。最初的几页填满了写作练习——俄语民歌的文本——正如波德卢布内所记，这些是他在1931年4月根据一个熟人的口述写下的。这些听写后面跟着波德卢布内自己创作的几段歌词。这些歌曲属于俄罗斯传统民间文化的范畴，围绕着年轻人的冒险和浪漫。波德卢布内写这些歌词可能是为了熟练掌握俄语，俄语在当时对他来说仍然是一门外语。正如他早期日记写作中随处可见的语法错误和乌克兰化表达所显示的，用俄语表达自己对他来说并不容易。

Podlubny began to write in his diary notebook just before he joined Pravda. The first pages were filled with writing exercises—texts of Russian folksongs—which, as Podlubny noted, were dictated to him by an acquaintance in April 1931. These dictations were followed by several more lyrics composed by Podlubny himself. The songs belonged to the repertoire of traditional Russian folk culture, revolving around young people’s adventures and romances. Podlubny probably wrote the lyrics to gain proficiency in Russian, which was still a foreign language for him at the time. As the many grammatical errors and Ukrainianisms dotting his early diary writing illustrate, expressing himself in Russian did not come easily.

真正的日记从笔记本后部开始，题目是《“共青团九大”旅的工作日记以及旅长兼学生斯捷潘·菲利波维奇·波德卢布内的每日笔记》。第一篇日记的日期是1931年5月31日。那天，波德卢布内被提名担任一个由十名工人组成的生产旅的旅长。接下来几天和几周的记录记载了个人成就——他被接纳加入共青团、被任命为墙报编辑——以及他所在旅的表现。斯捷潘特别记下了那些工作表现不理想的人。一位仅以姓氏辨认的女同事博罗达科几乎每天都会出现：她上班迟到，在工厂车间唱歌跳舞，或者在盥洗室洗漱花费过长时间。一篇谴责她态度的文章，题为《唱吧，博罗达科，唱吧……》出现在了墙报上。署名为“V”，这可能就是波德卢布内自己写的。他的日记记录了博罗达科的反应：“如果我知道这个‘V’是谁，我就一拳打在他的大脸上。”作为纠正博罗达科行为努力的一部分，波德卢布内派了两名女性生产旅成员去她家。她们发现她母亲是个“好人”，但对她的女儿无能为力，因为女儿“晚上在狂欢”并且“表现恶劣”。在共青团组织的模拟审判中，博罗达科受到了公开训诫；她的行为好转了几天，但很快又恢复了原样。
从他在莫斯科新生活的一开始，波德卢布内就积极投身于苏维埃政权推行的正常化政策中。他赞美纪律、社会主义竞赛和成就的规范，督促他的同事不仅要在工作中遵守这些规范，而且要在生活的各个领域采纳它们。博罗达科事件不得不使他意识到他自己的工作表现对他社会地位的重要性。如果他未能做出出色的工作，类似的背景调查可能会落到他头上。他的新生活是在一个受到严密监控的社会舞台上进行的。

The actual diary began on the back of the notebook and was entitled “Work Diary of the ‘9th-Komsomol-Congress’ Brigade and Daily Notes of the Brigadier and Student Stepan Filipovich Podlubny.” The first entry was dated May 31, 1931. On that day Podlubny had been nominated as leader of a brigade comprising ten workers. The entries of the following days and weeks recorded personal achievements—his acceptance into the Komsomol, his appointment as editor of a wall newspaper—as well as the performance of his brigade. Stepan noted in particular those whose work performance was unsatisfactory. One female co-worker, identified only by her last name, Borodako, came up almost daily: she would arrive late at work, sing and dance in the factory shop, or spend an inordinate amount of time washing herself in the bathroom. An article denouncing her attitude, entitled “Sing, Borodako, sing . . .” appeared in the wall newspaper. Signed “V.,” it was probably written by Podlubny himself. His diary records Borodako’s reaction: “If I knew who this ‘V.’ is, I would punch him in the mug.” As part of his efforts to rectify Borodako’s behavior, Podlubny sent two female brigade members to her home. They found her mother to be “a good person” but unable to do anything about her daughter, who was “carousing at night” and “behaving badly.” At a mock trial staged by the Komsomol, Borodako was publicly reprimanded; her behavior improved for a few days, but she soon reverted to her customary ways.

From the very beginning of his new life in Moscow Podlubny actively engaged himself in the policies of normalization practiced by the Soviet regime. He extolled the norms of discipline, socialist competition, and achievement, prodding his co-workers not only to conform to them at work but to adopt them in all spheres of life. The Borodako incident could not but make him aware of the importance of his own work performance for his standing in society. Should he fail to do outstanding work, a similar background check might be applied to him. His new life took place on an intensely monitored social stage.

从1932年开始，斯捷潘的日记改变了性质，转向记录他的个人希望、渴望和恐惧。他在一篇回顾性日记中解释说，早期的段落语调是“客观的”，并且“仅与工作场所相关”。他现在的任务是记述真正意义上的日记，“为了我全面发展的目的”。这种转变部分是由斯捷潘在加入《真理报》后不久报名的文学小组引起的。谈到这个小组，他告诫自己要写得更好，更流利并具有文学气息，这表明日记将成为这位立志成为作家的人的训练场。文学小组在第一个五年计划期间规模和成员激增。共产主义活动家和非共产主义作家都要求文学进入工业化运动，并为其动员和转型目标服务。工厂建立了自己的文学小组，经验丰富的作家在其中向无产阶级工人传授技艺，这些工人将成为社会主义建设和他们在工业化过程中自身转型的编年史家。

Starting in 1932, Stepan’s diary changed character, shifting toward a record of his personal hopes, longings, and fears. The earlier passages, he explained in a retrospective entry, had been “objective” in tone and had “related only to the workplace.” His task now was to keep a diary in the real sense, “for the purposes of my overall development.” This shift was in part induced by the literary circle in which Stepan had enrolled soon after joining Pravda. Referring to the circle, he admonished himself to write better, more fluently and in a literary vein, an indication that the diary was to be a training ground for the aspiring writer. Literary circles exploded in size and membership during the First Five-Year Plan. Communist activists and non-Communist writers alike called for literature to enter the industrialization campaign and serve its mobilizing and transformative goals. Factories established their own literary circles in which experienced writers imparted the skills of the craft to proletarian workers, who were to become chroniclers of both the building of socialism and their own transformation in the course of industrialization.

梦想成为一名作家的波德卢布内认为自己的任务是写一部个人回忆录，这也将是“1930年代”的一部“编年史”。他希望这部回忆录能以小说的形式记录他在苏维埃体制中作为一个富农后代的特殊经历。他甚至为这个项目想好了标题：“一个过时阶级的生活，及其精神重生和对新条件的适应”。波德卢布内提到了帮助他创作回忆录的范本：亚历山大·赫尔岑、列夫·托尔斯泰和马克西姆·高尔基的作品，这些俄罗斯自传传统的先行者在苏维埃体制中被视为“社会进步”作家而受到推崇。在回忆录中，他想要“记住生活，不仅是狭义上的家庭生活，还有政治事件的历程。并将这些届时已经过去的事件，同届时的现实相比；那样的现实如今还只是对未来的梦想。”

写作的时间越长，波德卢布内记日记的另一个动机就越发珍贵：日记已成了他“唯一的朋友”。只有对日记，他才能倾诉他过去的秘密以及伴随着他试图融入新社会的恐惧和怀疑。他的希望是通过将痛苦释放在纸上来解脱自己。日记充当了一个“垃圾堆”，他可以将积压在脑海中的所有“垃圾”丢弃在那里。在其他地方，他称日记为“我灵魂的镜子”，或者是一个揭示“一个人阴暗面”的媒介。波德卢布内的秘密及其在日记中的记录干扰了将日记用作文学训练场的预设用途。小组的其他成员大声朗读自己的日记并传阅。波德卢布内将自己的锁起来，甚至隐瞒其存在，因为他敏锐地意识到，如果日记落入错误的人手中，他会发生什么。

Dreaming of becoming a writer, Podlubny regarded it as his task to write a personal memoir that would also be a “chronicle” of the “1930s.” He wanted this memoir, which he planned to write in the form of a novel, to capture his specific experience as a kulak offspring in the Soviet system. He even had a title for the project: “the life of an outdated class, its spiritual rebirth and adaptation to new conditions.” Podlubny mentioned models that were to help him compose the memoir: works by Alexander Herzen, Leo Tolstoy, and Maxim Gorky, progenitors of the Russian autobiographical tradition who were held in high esteem in the Soviet system as “socially progressive” writers. In the memoir he wanted to “remember life, not just family life in the narrow sense, but also the course of political events. And compare these, by then already past events, with what happens in reality, which up to now is only a dream for the future.”

The longer he wrote, the more Podlubny cherished yet another motivation for keeping the diary: it had become his “sole friend.” Only to the diary could he confide the secret of his past and the fears and doubts that accompanied his attempt to fit into the new society. His hope was to free himself from his torments by releasing them on paper. The diary served as a “rubbish heap” onto which he could discard all the “garbage” that had accumulated in his mind. Elsewhere he referred to the diary as the “mirror of my soul,” or as a medium revealing “the seamy side of a person.” Podlubny’s secret and his recording of it in his diary interfered with the projected use of the diary as a literary training ground. Other members of the circle read aloud from their diaries and showed them around. Podlubny kept his own locked away and even concealed its existence, being acutely aware of what might happen to him if it fell into the wrong hands.

虽然被用于各种目的——作为无用思想的“垃圾堆”、培养意识的训练场、情感释放的源泉、最好的朋友——波德卢布内的日记也服务于一个首要目的。它是他自我的实验室。在排除“阴暗”思想的过程中变得更纯洁的愿望，与他那显然不那么阴暗的回忆录的目的平行展开。这两个项目都将为他宣称拥有苏维埃社会成员身份提供证据，并且两者都与他个人争取道德自我完善的斗争紧密相连。在这个寻找政治融合、社会接纳和自尊的阶级异己的项目中，公共和私人的目标被有效地融合在了一起。

While deployed for various ends—as “rubbish heap” for useless thoughts, training ground for developing consciousness, emotional source of relief, best friend—Podlubny’s diary also served an overarching purpose. It was a laboratory of his self. The desire to become purer in the course of discharging his “black” thoughts ran parallel to the purpose of his decidedly less black memoirs. Both projects were to provide evidence for his claim to membership in Soviet society, and both were tied to his personal struggle for moral self-improvement. Public and private ends were effectively fused in this project of a class alien in search of political integration, social acceptance, and self-respect.

zh: 富农出身的问题
en: The Problem of the Kulak Past

children: 波德卢布内模糊的社会地位，源于布尔什维克对富农后代及其他阶级异己分子的态度中一种未解决的紧张关系。整个新经济政策时期，苏维埃国家勉强接受了一个阶级社会的存在，包括“旧的”、“封建资本主义”秩序的残余。然而，在政治上，富农以及前牧师、警察和地主都被剥夺了选举权。

当政权开始其激进的工业化运动时，一项官方决定是“消灭富农作为一个阶级”。其理由是，在一个无阶级的社会主义社会中，没有资本主义剥削者的容身之地。从1929至1930年冬天开始，被认定为“富农”的农民家庭的财产被系统地没收，数百万富农被遣送到行政流放地。富农群体被分为三类，根据他们据称对苏维埃政权构成的危险程度。第一类成员，“反革命富农积极分子”，被认为是不可救药、顽固不化的苏维埃制度敌人，他们中有数千人被处决。第二类和第三类富农，被认为政治活动不那么活跃，因此危险性较小，根据他们反苏态度的程度，被流放到较近或较远的地区。

Podlubny’s ambiguous social standing resulted from an unresolved tension in Bolshevik attitudes toward kulak descendants and other class aliens. Throughout the New Economic Policy period, the Soviet state grudgingly accepted the existence of a class society, including remnants of the “old,” “feudal-capitalist” order. Politically, however, kulaks as well as former priests, policemen, and landowners were disenfranchised.

When the regime embarked on its radical industrialization campaign, an official decision was reached to “eliminate the kulaks as a class.” The rationale was that in a classless socialist society there would be no place for capitalist exploiters. Beginning in the winter of 1929–30, the property of peasant households deemed “kulak” was systematically expropriated and several million kulaks were deported into administrative exile. The kulak peasantry was divided into three categories, according to the degree of danger they allegedly posed to Soviet power. Members of the first group, the “counterrevolutionary kulak aktiv,” were deemed incorrigible, inveterate enemies of the Soviet system, and thousands of them were executed. Kulaks of the second and third categories, considered less politically active and hence less dangerous, were exiled to nearer or more distant localities depending on the degree of their anti-Soviet attitudes.

1930年代初期的苏联法律规定，后两类富农如果能证明他们为苏维埃国家诚实劳动了至少五年，就可以恢复权利。因此，该政权原则上并不反对前富农，特别是他们的家属融入社会，前提是他们证明自己已经摆脱了阶级异己的本质。这些法律基于个人可以通过自身努力改造自己的信念，表达了布尔什维克意识形态的普遍主义主张。这解释了为什么苏联官员不愿通过血统来确定阶级身份，以免富农的儿子永远被贴上富农的标签。阶级归属首先是个人意志的一种品质，而不论其社会出身。波德卢布内——像许多其他阶级异己分子一样——在工厂寻求工作时，坚持这种意志主义的阶级解释。他希望通过在无产阶级环境中工作，通过“在工人熔炉中熬炼”，他可以摆脱富农本质，净化自己，并获得一个真正的无产者思想。
然而，布尔什维克意识形态的这种整合倾向，却受到苏联日常生活中针对阶级异己分子的一系列歧视性做法的阻碍。20世纪30年代中期以前，他们被禁止接受高等教育，并始终面临被解雇的风险。这些态度源于一种怀疑，认为阶级异己分子本质上反对苏联秩序，无法完全改造自己成为忠诚的公民。该政权发起了疯狂的警惕运动，试图揭露那些被认为藏匿在工厂、高等教育机构和国家行政部门的阶级异己分子。
波德卢布内的日记显示，他对国家发出的复杂信号也以同样复杂的方式回应。他知道自己必须隐瞒过去，从而进行某种形式的外在伪装，这种需求每当政权加强镇压措施时，就变得尤为迫切。同时，他欣喜地留意每一个迹象，只要迹象表明阶级异己分子真诚为社会主义国家工作就可能获得救赎。然而，在寻求融入社会时，他面临一个相当大的问题：他隐瞒背景的行为，必然会被当局解读为颠覆性和反革命的。
更糟糕的是，隐瞒与转变相结合的策略，削弱了波德卢布内对自己真诚的信念。他对新身份的矛盾心理体现在他构思中的小说标题《阶级异己分子的“精神重生与适应”》中。如果说第一个词组预示着真正的内在转变，那么第二个词组则暗示着对一个性质不同的现实的适应，从而对转变的追求的有效性提出了疑问。

Soviet laws of the early 1930s stipulated that kulaks in the last two categories could be rehabilitated if they demonstrated that they had performed at least five years of honest labor for the Soviet state. The regime was thus not in principle opposed to the integration of former kulaks and especially their dependents into the social body, provided that they proved they had shed their class-alien essence. Resting on the belief that individuals could remake themselves through their own efforts, these laws expressed the universalist pretense of Bolshevik ideology. This explains why Soviet officials showed themselves reluctant to determine class identity genealogically, so that the son of a kulak would also be branded forever a kulak. Membership in a social class was first and foremost a quality of individuals’ will, regardless of their social origins. Podlubny—like many other class aliens—clung to this voluntarist interpretation of class in seeking work in a factory. He hoped that by working in a proletarian environment, by “stewing in the workers’ cauldron,” he could shed his kulak essence, purify himself, and acquire the ideology of a true proletarian.

Yet this integrative orientation of Bolshevik ideology was counteracted by a host of discriminatory practices against class aliens in Soviet daily life. Up to the mid-1930s they were barred from higher education and perennially at risk of being dismissed from their jobs. These attitudes were rooted in a suspicion that class aliens were inherently opposed to the Soviet order and could not completely remake themselves into loyal citizens. The regime engaged in frantic vigilance campaigns and attempts to unmask class aliens who were believed to be hiding in factories, institutes of higher education, and the state administration.

Podlubny’s diary shows that he responded to the mixed signals of the state in equally complex ways. He knew he had to conceal his past and thus engage in some form of outward dissimulation, a need that was especially acute whenever the regime stepped up its repressive measures. At the same time, he exuberantly noted every indication that class aliens might redeem themselves if they worked sincerely for the socialist state. Yet in seeking integration he faced a considerable problem: his concealment of his background was bound to be interpreted by the authorities as subversive and counterrevolutionary.

Making things even worse, the combined strategy of concealment and transformation undermined Podlubny’s own sense of his sincerity. His ambivalence about his new identity showed in the title of his projected novel on the class alien’s “spiritual rebirth and adaptation.” If the first term signaled genuine inner transformation, the second suggested accommodation to a qualitatively different reality, and thus raised questions about the validity of the quest for transformation.

在他在莫斯科的岁月里，除了20世纪30年代中期短暂的平静期，波德卢布内一直生活在猎捕隐藏的阶级异己分子和政治反革命者的“猎巫”气氛中。这种“布尔什维克警惕性”如何在日常生活中实践，可以从煤矿工人弗拉基米尔·莫洛佐夫的日记中一窥究竟。对热心的共青团员莫洛佐夫来说，一位农民出身的工友的态度，激发了他揭露其富农身份的冲动：“我与苏沃洛夫谈论生产，他宣称：‘我来这里是为了多挣钱，给自己置办家当。’这就是农民心理！只看到个人利益，只相信自己。诚然，并非所有农民都是这样……新的集体农庄正在教育新人。我刚想到：苏沃洛夫会不会是富农的爪牙，是不是被派来这里瓦解工人士气？一切皆有可能。”几天后，莫洛佐夫注意到他未能证实对苏沃洛夫的怀疑。接下来，他把怒火转向了另一位农民工人，此人从村里收到了一包猪肉——这无疑表明了他富农的出身。这位同事给了莫洛佐夫一些肉，然后向他要了烟草作为回报。莫洛佐夫勃然大怒：“整个故事让我清楚地看到了富农是如何收买农民的……但你们休想收买我们，我们现在能看穿富农的灵魂。”

Throughout his years in Moscow, except for a brief lull in the mid-1930s, Podlubny lived in an atmosphere of witch hunt against hidden class aliens and political counterrevolutionaries. How such “Bolshevik vigilance” was practiced in daily life can be gleaned from the diary of the coal miner Vladimir Molodtsov. For the ardent komsomolist Molodtsov, the attitude of a fellow worker of peasant background sparked an urge to unmask him as a kulak: “I got into a conversation about production with Suvorov, and he declared: ‘I’ve come here to earn more money and equip myself.’ There it is, the peasant psychology! Sees only his personal gain and believes only in himself. True, not all of the peasantry is like this . . . The new kolkhozes are educating new people. I just had a thought: Isn’t Suvorov perhaps a kulak henchman, wasn’t he sent here to demoralize the workers? Anything is possible.” A few days later Molodtsov noted that he had not been able to confirm his suspicions about Suvorov. He next directed his ire toward another peasant worker who had received a package of pork from his village—a sure indication of his kulak origins. This colleague gave Molodtsov some of the meat, then asked him for tobacco in return. Molodtsov was furious: “This whole story has given me a clear picture of how the kulak buys off the peasantry . . . Only you won’t buy us off, we can now see through a kulak’s soul.”

波德卢布内的日记也谈到了同样的问题，但却是从另一个角度。它记录了一个人发现自己被敌人包围的恐惧，这些敌人正等着揭露他新获得的身份是虚假的。鉴于他们的警惕性，任何一个紧张的姿态或失言都可能带来灾难性的后果。当波德卢布内的共青团小组在莫斯科附近的一个集体农庄组织夏令营时，他作为小组长建议大家黎明前起床，工作到上午十一点，然后休息到下午晚些时候以避开烈日。其他想睡晚一点的人不同意，但他的提议最终得以实施。在日记中，波德卢布内自责自己的立场。别人可能会怀疑他出身农村，然后调查他的背景。他决定接下来的几天工作得更马虎一些，以免显得像一个熟练的农民工人。

他的日记里充满了提醒，告诫自己不要屈服于向朋友和同事倾诉个人问题和担忧的冲动。这些冲动是“多余的”和危险的，因为它们会让别人窥探到他那充满问题的内心生活。更令人担忧的是与那些在他以前生活中认识他的人的相遇。有一次在街上，斯捷潘和他的母亲碰到了“沃瓦和伊塔”，他们是以前的邻居，从乌克兰逃荒来到莫斯科。波德卢布内一家帮助他们在城里找到了住所。斯捷潘报告说，虽然他很高兴见到家乡的人，但也感觉到了这种接触的危险：“如果你不能阻止自己说出对你不利的话，那就别指望控制别人多嘴多舌。你所能做的就是等着看。我的手脚都被束缚住了。这不好，一点都不好。”与此同时，波德卢布内渴望了解周围的人在谈论什么、思考什么，以便尽可能快地察觉潜在危险并做出反应。他时刻提醒自己要“专业谨慎和善于观察”，他与莫洛佐夫一样，都在从事着相同的怀疑诠释学，只不过在他这里，这些是用来保护自己免受布尔什维克警惕的。
另一种在新社会环境中驾驭险恶局面的方式，是模仿那些看起来强大而受欢迎的人的行为。波德卢布内相信，一旦他获得了同他们一样的“威望”，他就会变得不那么脆弱。在日记的早期部分，一位共青团书记就是这样的榜样：“我精确地模仿他的行动和举止。”后来，他被工厂学校的校长取代，斯捷潘称校长为“我每天都热切地照的镜子”。

波德卢布内的适应技巧被证明非常成功。无论是在学校还是在工作中，他很快就脱颖而出，成为一名模范学徒。他的成功体现在工厂学校的优异成绩、在共青团管理部门崭露头角的职业生涯，以及他对自己获得了同伴中“威望”的满足感。1931年秋天，在他加入《真理报》几个月后，他的照片刊登在工厂报纸上，表彰他作为班组长和突击队员的成就。其他照片展示了波德卢布内抵达莫斯科后所经历的显著外在变化。在1929年他小学毕业班的合影中，那个看起来比同学们更年轻、更瘦小的农家少年，到1932年冬天已经变成了一个穿着时髦的城市青年。1932年的照片显示波德卢布内与《真理报》印刷厂的两名工友在一起。他左边的同事（照片右侧）穿着村民的毡靴；另一位学徒的衣领凌乱。站在中间的波德卢布内是这群人中穿着最得体、最整洁的，他也表现出最强的自信。当然，三人戴着类似的软帽，以显得像是见多识广的城市青年。在一张1934年波德卢布内与“真理报学校红旗五班”同学的合影中，斯捷潘·波德卢布内是唯一一个穿着西装打领带的人。他和其他一名学生夹克上戴着徽章，可能是因体育或“突击工作”而获得的奖章。

Podlubny’s diary addressed the same issue, but from the other side. It documented the fear of a person who saw himself surrounded by enemies waiting to expose his newly claimed identity as a sham. Given their watchfulness, any nervous gesture or slip of the tongue could have catastrophic consequences. When Podlubny’s Komsomol group organized a summer camp on a kolkhoz near Moscow, he as a group leader suggested that everyone get up before dawn, work until eleven a.m., and then break until late afternoon to avoid the scorching sun. Others, who wanted to sleep later in the morning, disagreed, but his position prevailed. In his diary Podlubny reproached himself for his stance. Others might suspect that he was of rural background, and then investigate his background. He resolved to work more sloppily the next few days so as to not appear to be a skilled peasant worker.

His diary was filled with reminders not to give in to urges to confide personal problems and worries to friends and colleagues. These impulses were “superfluous” and dangerous, as they allowed others glimpses into his problematic inner life. Even more worrying were encounters with people who had known him in his prior life. On the street Stepan and his mother once ran into “Vova and Itta,” former neighbors who had come to Moscow to flee the famine raging in Ukraine. The Podlubnys helped them find shelter in the city. Stepan reported that while he was happy to see people from back home, he also sensed the danger of such contacts: “If you can’t prevent yourself from spilling words that are harmful to you, forget about controlling others’ flapping tongues. All you can do is wait and see. My arms and my legs are tied. This is not good, not good at all.” At the same time, Podlubny was eager to know what the people around him talked about and thought, so as to sense potential danger and react as quickly as possible. Reminding himself always to be “professionally cautious and observant,” he was engaged in the same hermeneutics of suspicion as Molodtsov, except that in his case they served as protection from Bolshevik vigilance.

Another way to navigate the treacherous terrain of his new social environment was to emulate the behavior of people who appeared strong and popular. Once he had gained their “authority,” Podlubny believed, he would be less vulnerable. In the early parts of the diary a Komsomol secretary figured as such a role model: “I exactly copy his actions and manners.” In later years he was replaced by the director of the factory school, whom Stepan called the “mirror into which I avidly look every day.”

Podlubny’s adaptive techniques proved highly successful. Both in school and at work he soon stood out as a model apprentice. His successes showed in good grades at the factory school, a budding career in the Komsomol administration, and his own satisfaction at having acquired “authority” among his peers. In the fall of 1931, a few months after he joined Pravda, his picture appeared in the factory newspaper, acknowledging his achievements as brigade leader and shock worker. Other photographs demonstrate the remarkable outward change that Podlubny underwent after his arrival in Moscow. The peasant boy, who in a 1929 shot of his primary school graduating class appears younger and smaller than his classmates, by the winter of 1932 had turned into a fashionably dressed, urban young man. The 1932 photo shows Podlubny with two fellow workers from the Pravda printing plant. The colleague on his left (at right in the photo) wears the felt boots of a villager; the other apprentice’s collar is disheveled. Standing in the middle, Podlubny appears as the best dressed and groomed of the group, and he also conveys the most self-assurance. All three, to be sure, wear similar soft caps to pass as sophisticated young urbanites. In a 1934 photograph of Podlubny with classmates from “Red Banner class no. 5 of the Pravda school,” he is the only man wearing a suit and tie. He and one other student wear badges on their jackets, possibly medals awarded for sports or “shock work.”
这些照片只讲述了波德卢布内人生故事的一部分。正如他的日记清楚表明，他在工作上的成功并未能有效缓解他的焦虑。外在适应新环境对他生存至关重要，但这不足以解决他作为阶级异己的困境。对他来说，更根本的挑战是内在的改变，重塑他的内心倾向，使其与他作为社会主义国家公民的外在形象相符。这种自我改变远不止是换上新衣服那么简单。

The photographs tell only part of Podlubny’s life story. As his diary  makes clear, his successes at work did little to alleviate his anxieties. Outward conformity to his new environment was indispensable for his survival, but it was insufficient to resolve his problematic standing as a class alien. The more fundamental challenge for him was to change in-wardly, to remake his inner disposition to match his outward appearance as a citizen of the socialist state. This type of self-change involved far more than donning new clothes.

波德卢布内在日记中阐述了他的内心倾向问题，这篇日记专门讨论了他在印刷厂的工作表现。他假定，对于社会主义国家中的一个真正无产者来说，劳动是自然实现自我的领域，因此毫不费力，他想知道为什么工作会让他付出如此大的努力：
我在生产工作上的成功并没有让我感到高兴。一个我似乎永远无法摆脱的想法，像从桦树中吸取树液一样，从我身上吸走我的血液，那就是我的“心理”问题。难道我真的与众不同吗？这个问题让我毛骨悚然，不寒而栗。现在，我是一个居中之人，不属于任何一方，但很容易滑向任何一个方向。但积极的一面占据主导地位的机会已经更大——只是仍然带着一丝消极的残留。这一丝[消极的]东西是如何恶毒地折磨着我。
他问题的根源在于他的“心理”，这与莫洛佐夫在他怀疑是伪装成富农的矿工同伴身上发现的力量相同。这个词指的是个体内部未被组织的精神-身体力量；“心理”是在个体有意识地组织自我之前构成个人的东西。在波德卢布内的案例中，“心理”指的是他作为富农之子，深受乡村文化熏陶的背景所形成的塑造性影响。从这“出身和记忆的旧伤”中，流淌出他内心所有不好的、反动的、落后的东西。
波德卢布内暗示，他这种消极的自我就是内在的阶级敌人，威胁要占据他的思想。但他也有积极的一面，由意识的力量代表，这种力量可以塑造和转化心理。增强意识是获得无产阶级身份，从而成为一个新人的方式。波德卢布内正处于“中间”，介于他被否定了的过去和他所期望的未来身份之间。

Podlubny articulated the problem of his inner disposition in a diary entry devoted to his work performance at the printing plant. Assuming that for a real proletarian in a socialist state, labor was an arena of natural self-realization and thus effortless, he wondered why work cost him so much effort:

My successes in production work don’t make me happy. A thought that I can never seem to shake off, that sucks my blood from me like sap from a birch tree, is the question of my psychology. Can it really be that I am different from the others? This question makes my hair stand on end, and I break out in shivers. Right now, I am a person in the middle, not belonging to one side or the other, but who could easily slip in either direction. But the chances are already greater for the positive side to take over—but still with a touch of the negative left. How devilishly this touch [of the negative] torments me.

At the root of his problem was his “psychology,” the same force that Molodtsov had identified in his fellow miner whom he suspected of being a kulak in disguise. The word referred to the unorganized psychic-physical forces working inside the individual; psychology was what constituted an individual before his conscious self-organization. In Podlubny’s case, “psychology” referred to the shaping influence of his background as a kulak’s son steeped in village culture. From this “old wound of my origins and memories” flowed everything that was bad, reactionary, backward inside him.

Podlubny implied that this negative side of his self was the inner class enemy who threatened to take possession of him. But there was also a positive side in him, represented by the forces of consciousness, which could mold and transform psychology. Strengthening consciousness was the way to acquire a proletarian identity and thus to become a new man. Podlubny stood “in the middle,” between his discredited past and his anticipated future identity.

发展意识的一种方式是阅读并内化苏联的基本文献：“我问政治学习小组的负责人：‘我应该先读马克思还是列宁？’他说我应该同时阅读两者。这非常重要。他建议我用铅笔做批注。在马克思的哲学中，他说了很多晦涩难懂的东西，其中有太多难以理解之处，有如此的深度，以至于你读了第三遍仍然会发现一些新的意义。”

然而，几周后，波德卢布内带着一种徒劳感，将马克思从他的阅读计划中删除。他在阅读小说、参观博物馆和剧院方面表现出更大的毅力——期望从中找到指导自己思想和行为的方针。一个特别令人失望的经历是阅读高尔基的三卷本《克利姆·萨姆金的一生》。波德卢布内钦佩高尔基是苏联领先的作家，也是主张阶级异己分子可以通过劳动改造的提倡者。然而，他发现这部小说“枯燥、单调、模糊”，并对萨姆金在整本书中始终是一个“未定义”的人物感到遗憾。波德卢布内期望在苏联文化中找到决心的榜样和清晰的思维方式，而不仅仅是他仍在过着的“不确定”和“无系统”生活的翻版。
在波德卢布内对自我变化的理解中，内在欲望与外在适应的需求紧密交织。转变的强制性和自愿性维度，在他回顾乡村旧生活的日记中得到了很好的表达：那时“没有任何外部或内部力量干预我的命运”。他的措辞暗示，集体化的外部强制影响，在他内心激发了自我更新的渴望。他补充说，在过去，“他的视野[一直]非常非常狭窄。”自那以后的岁月见证了“我生活和境况的重建”。

One way to develop consciousness was to read and internalize the fundamental Soviet texts: “[I] asked the leader of the political circle: What should I read first, Marx or Lenin? He said I should read both at the same time. That is very significant. He advised me to work with a pencil. In Marx, in his philosophy, he says so many obscure things, so much in it is difficult to understand, there are such depths, that you read it for the third time and still discover some new meaning.”

A few weeks later, however, expressing a sense of futility, Podlubny dropped Marx from his agenda. He showed greater perseverance in reading novels and going to museums and theaters—expecting to find guidelines for his own thought and behavior. A particularly disappointing experience was reading the three volumes of Gorky’s The Life of Klim Samgin. Podlubny admired Gorky as the leading Soviet writer and as a proponent of the idea that class aliens could be reeducated through labor. Yet he found the novel “boring, monotonous, and foggy,” and deplored the fact that Samgin remained an “undefined” person throughout the book. Podlubny expected to find in Soviet culture models of determination and a clear way to think, not merely replicas of the “indeterminable” and “unsystematic” life he was still leading.

Inner desire and the need to adapt outwardly were densely interwoven in Podlubny’s understanding of self-change. The combined coercive and self-willed dimension of transformation is well stated in a retrospective entry devoted to his former life in the village, “when no external or internal forces whatsoever intervened in my fate.” The external, coercive impact of collectivization, his wording suggests, un-leashed in him an inner desire for self-renewal. Back in the old days, he added, his “horizon [had been] very, very narrow.” The years since had witnessed the “reconstruction of my life and situation.”

然而，当他从过去转向现在和未来时，波德卢布内对个人转变的前景信心不足。特别是，他仍然不确定自己的心理根深蒂固到何种程度，或者有多容易改变。即使是他为了自我更新而进行的掌握文化计划，也可以被解读为一种阶级异己分子特有的过度文化迷恋。这种怀疑和自我不信任在1933年末浮出水面，当时波德卢布内从车间调到了印刷厂图书馆。他写道，他儿时的一个梦想实现了：被书籍环绕，在一个“有文化”的环境中工作，与受过教育的同事为伴。此外，这次调动也使他更接近实现成为作家的目标。但波德卢布内担心背离工厂车间的含义。

As he turned from the past to the present and future, however, Podlubny was less confident of the prospects of personal transformation. In particular, he remained uncertain about how ingrained or amenable to change his psychology was. Even his program of mastering culture, conducted for the purpose of self-renewal, could be read as an inordinate obsession with culture characteristic of class aliens. Such doubts and self-distrust came to the fore in late 1933, when Podlubny transferred from the shop floor to the library of the printing plant. He wrote that a dream dating back to his childhood had come true: to be surrounded by books and work in a “cultured” environment, in the company of educated colleagues. Furthermore, the transfer had brought him closer to the realization of his goal to become a writer. But Podlubny worried about the implications of turning his back on the factory shop floor.
在那里，他曾身处工人阶级行列，在那里，获得无产阶级意识几乎是板上钉钉的事。相比之下，图书馆是一个吸引寻求在苏联社会中找到一席之地的阶级异己分子的避风港。波德卢布内担心，国家会特别在图书馆这样的地方寻找敌人，而且他的新工作场所提供的社会有用工作的机会较少，因此改造的机会也较少：
无论你喂狼多少，它仍然向往森林。我就是这样。无论我如何努力改造自己，我就是摆脱不掉一个无用之人的习惯。确实，这些习惯很微小，甚至外人察觉不到，但当我审视自己时，一切都显而易见。我多么小心翼翼，我注意自己说的话，但仅仅一个根深蒂固的习惯就可能毁掉我，也许是永远。
在他学习和改造自己的新生活几年后，波德卢布内在某种程度上仍然认为自己是披着羊皮的狼。部分原因在于重塑根深蒂固的心理这一任务的巨大性和难以捉摸性。更重要的是，他的自我改造计划是在苏联国家镇压措施下展开的，这些措施迫使他隐藏，从而保留了他希望摆脱的狼性本质。

There he had been in the ranks of the working class, where the attainment of proletarian consciousness was virtually guaranteed. The library, by contrast, was a haven that attracted class aliens seeking a niche in Soviet society. Podlubny was concerned both that the state would look for enemies especially in places like the library, and that his new workplace afforded less opportunity for socially useful work and hence for reeducation:

No matter how much you feed the wolf, he still looks to the forest. It’s the same with me. No matter how much I try to reeducate myself, I simply can’t get rid of the habits of a useless person. It’s true that they are small, not even noticeable to an outsider, but to me when I observe myself everything is noticeable. How careful I am, I watch what I say, but just one ingrained habit could be the end of me, perhaps forever.

Several years into his new life of learning and remaking himself, Podlubny still believed himself in some sense to be a wolf in disguise. In part this had to do with the very magnitude and elusiveness of the task of reforging an ingrained psychology. Even more important, his project of self-change unfolded amid repressive measures of the Soviet state that forced him to hide, and thus retain, the very wolflike nature that he wished to shed.

zh: 主体性与国家

children: 在他的日记早期，波德卢布内描述了学到的一个重要教训，他指出，这种教训你不会在教科书中读到，而只能在现实生活中经历。背景是《真理报》印刷厂，那里经常因未经培训或疲惫的工人操作技术设备不当而导致停工。这些生产中断通常伴随着揭露意图颠覆苏维埃政权的“破坏分子”的呼声。作为负责一支混合工人群体的班组长，波德卢布内处于一个暴露的境地。此外，他不断受到一位老技术指导的骚扰，这位指导显然无法忍受他热情直率的共青团积极性。波德卢布内将印刷厂形容为“蛇窝”，里面充满了等待指控他为破坏者和阶级敌人的“敌人”。在一次他被指控损坏机器并受到共青团书记训斥的事件后，波德卢布内决定他发现了一条基本法则：“我已经摸索出一种新的人生方法……你必须时刻顾及国家利益，特别是生产利益，而不是随大流，让自己被他们污染。”

波德卢布内将国家视为决定他命运的终极力量。无论是在生产过程中，作为共青团积极分子，还是在学校里，他都是为国家工作，国家也以此为基础决定他的身份。他相信，为“国家利益”持续工作将使他免于成为工作场所阴谋的受害者，并最终确保他融入苏联体系。在日记中，波德卢布内将国家描述为一种外部的，甚至是敌对的力量，他必须像一个渺小而始终容易受伤的生灵一样去适应它。但他表达了希望，总有一天他有问题的阶级身份会自行解决，使他能够出于真诚的个人信念认同苏维埃国家的利益。

Early on in his diary, Podlubny described learning an important lesson, a lesson of the kind that, he noted, you did not read about in textbooks but experienced only in real life. The setting was the Pravda print shop, a place where work stoppages caused by mishandling of technical equipment by untrained or exhausted workers were frequent. These breakdowns in production were habitually followed by calls to unmask the “saboteurs” intent on bringing down Soviet power. As a brigade leader responsible for a mixed team of workers, Podlubny was in an exposed position. Furthermore, he kept being harassed by an old technical instructor who apparently could not stand his ardent and outspoken Komsomol activism. Podlubny characterized the print shop as a “snake pit” filled with “enemies” waiting to denounce him as a wrecker and a class enemy. After an incident in which he had been accused of damaging a machine and reprimanded by the Komsomol secretary, Podlubny decided he had discovered a fundamental rule: “I’ve worked out a new approach to life . . . You always have to reach out to the interests of the state, and of production in particular, and not follow the moods of the other guys and let yourself be contaminated by them.”

Podlubny experienced the state as the ultimate force that decided his fate. It was for the state that he worked, whether in the production process, as a Komsomol activist, or in school, and on this basis the state determined his very identity. Persistent work for the “interests of the state,” he believed, would save him from falling victim to the in-trigues at the workplace and ultimately assure him integration into the Soviet system. In diary entries Podlubny described the state as an external and, indeed, hostile force, to which he had to adapt as a small and always vulnerable creature. But he also expressed hope that one day his problematic class identity would resolve itself, enabling him to identify with the interests of the Soviet state out of genuine personal conviction.

这位《真理报》印刷厂的年轻学徒，在他提出融入社会希望的时候，政权在清除苏联社会中不良分子方面，远比接纳阶级异己分子更积极。在1932至1933年秋冬发生的两组事件中，这一点对波德卢布内来说变得非常清楚。1932年10月，秘密警察（格别乌）的官员找到他，要求他为他们当一名告密者。格别乌很可能注意到波德卢布内，是因为他作为班组长和共青团积极分子的出色表现。这种讽刺意味非凡：为了隐瞒他有问题的过去，波德卢布内作为一名苏联积极分子表现出色，而正是基于他的成功，格别乌委托这位“共青团员”——这是分配给他的代号——去揭露像他自己一样的伪装阶级敌人。

The young apprentice in the Pravda print shop outlined his hopes for integration at a time when the regime was far more active in weeding Soviet society of unwanted elements than in inviting class aliens into its fold. This was made dramatically clear to Podlubny in two sets of events in the fall and winter of 1932–33. In October 1932 he was approached by officers of the secret police (GPU), who asked him to work for them as an informer. In all likelihood the GPU had taken notice of Podlubny because of his outstanding record as brigade leader and Komsomol activist. The irony was remarkable: in an effort to conceal his problematic past, Podlubny excelled as a Soviet activist, and on the basis of his success the GPU entrusted the “komsomolist”—this was the code name assigned to him—with the task of unmasking disguised class enemies just like himself.
作为一名告密者，波德卢布内会定期在不同地点与他的格别乌联络官见面——或在看门人的公寓里，或在秘密警察总部。他必须签署一份文件，同意条款并承诺保守其任务的秘密。在他被招募几天后写的一篇简短日记中，波德卢布内对“卷入”格别乌表示遗憾，这个措辞暗示了他某种程度的积极配合，以及他本可以拒绝他们提议的可能性，尽管现在已无法挽回。
但他同意担任告密者与他始终捍卫国家利益的哲学是一致的。背弃格别乌可能会损害该组织对他作为一名忠诚苏联公民的印象，并可能引起更深远的怀疑。

As an informant Podlubny would meet with his GPU contact officer periodically and at different places—either in janitors’ apartments or at the secret police headquarters. He had to sign a document agreeing to the terms and promising to keep his assignment secret. In a short diary entry written a few days after his recruitment, Podlubny voiced regret over having “involved himself” with the GPU, a word choice that suggests a degree of active compliance on his part and the possibility, forgone by now, that he could have turned down their offer.

But his agreement to work as an informant was consistent with his philosophy of always defending the interests of the state. Turning his back on the GPU would have risked undermining the organization’s impression of him as a devoted Soviet citizen and might have aroused even more far-reaching suspicions.

但他与秘密警察的接触使他的生活极度紧张。控制每一个字眼和每一个姿态的需求变得更加强烈，他现在正与那个专门揭露他这种人的权力机关打交道。1932年11月的一则日记描述了他和母亲坐在他们的地下室公寓里，面前的桌子上放着一张传票：“也许这是我们最后一次坐在一起的夜晚了，到了那里[在格别乌会议上]，我们会被拆散。一个人将不知道另一个人的情况（妈妈）。可怕。糟糕透了，但却是开玩笑似地说出来，笑着。啊，去吧！我们是命运手中的玩物，正如老谚语所说。快到凌晨两点了，但我们甚至没有想过睡觉。”第二天，当斯捷潘离开去回应传票时，他的母亲穿着五条裙子，已经收拾好了她的物品。如果他不回来，她就打算逃走，到阿尔汉格尔斯克与她被流放的丈夫团聚。斯捷潘被传唤的会议结果是例行公事。

波德卢布内与秘密警察打交道，而秘密警察比任何其他国家组织都更能体现革命的净化原则，这不断地提醒着他自己的不纯洁出身。格别乌促使他以他想避免的精确术语来思考自己，即私人思想与外在行为之间的对立。这种分裂的心态与那种思想和行为统一、出于内在信念的综合社会主义人格相去甚远：“我日常的隐秘性和我内心生活的秘密不允许我成为一个具有独立性格的人。我不能公开或尖锐地表达任何自由思想。相反，我只能说所有人都在说的话……不知不觉中，我正在形成一种谄媚者、一条狡猾的狗的性格：温顺、懦弱，总是屈服。多么陈腐，多么令人作呕！”

波德卢布内为格别乌所做的工作并非完全是隐瞒和适应。他写的关于《真理报》工厂年轻工人“情绪”的报告，其观察结果早于他被招募为情报员。他的1932年日记反复提到他所在班组的一名成员，一个名叫阿尼辛的工人。五月份，阿尼辛因为排版了一个反革命口号而引起了丑闻。当共青团调查阿尼辛的背景时，波德卢布内作为班组长受到了训斥。那年晚些时候，也参加文学圈的阿尼辛，向波德卢布内朗读了他日记中的一些片段。波德卢布内将这些段落解释为阿尼辛性格的直接表达，感到震惊：“我们的写作方式多么不同。他真是个利己主义者。太令人惊讶了。他想成为一个对周围环境漠不关心的人。那真是死气沉沉的无聊。确实，他是一个不确定的人，确实，很难说他是什么样的人，你搞不清楚他的想法。”十一月，格别乌指派波德卢布内观察阿尼辛，阿尼辛当时已被共青团开除。波德卢布内的报告未能找到，但他在日记中将阿尼辛的行为描述为“可疑和欺骗性的”，无缝地阐述了他对这位“不确定”的同事的早期看法。

工厂里的年轻工人中，“反革命”情绪普遍存在，波德卢布内在日记中写道。他呼吁格别乌介入并加强其“教育工作”。他将秘密警察描绘成一个道德权威，其职责是纠正犯错个体的意识，从而恢复他们破碎的心理健康。波德卢布内还支持格别乌对社会卫生的关注。他曾向他的联系官员报告说，他在公园里被一个想与他发生性关系的男人搭讪。波德卢布内提供了那个男人的名字，他特意弄到了这个名字。格别乌对此案表示兴趣，并告诉他嫌疑人很快就会被“揭露”。波德卢布内的报告不仅限于苏联青年的道德健康。

But his encounters with the secret police strained his life to an extreme. The need to control every word and every gesture was intensified now that he dealt face to face with the very authority that specialized in unmasking people like him. A diary entry of November 1932 describes him and his mother sitting in their basement apartment with a summons lying on the table in front of them: “Perhaps it’s the last evening that we are sitting together, and there [at the GPU meeting], we’ll be torn apart. One will not know of the other (Mama). Terrifying. Awful, but said as a joke, laughing. Ah, here goes! We are toys in fate’s hands, as the old proverb says. Almost two a.m., but we don’t even think of sleeping.” By the time Stepan left to answer the summons the next day, his mother, wearing five skirts, had packed up her belongings. If he did not come back she was going to escape and rejoin her exiled husband in Arkhangelsk. The meeting to which Stepan was summoned turned out to be routine.

Podlubny’s dealings with the secret police, which more than any other state organization incarnated the revolutionary principle of purification, constantly reminded him of his own impure origins. The GPU prompted him to think of himself in precisely the terms he wanted to avoid, namely, in an opposition between private thoughts and outward behavior. This resulting split mind was a far cry from the integrated socialist personality who thought and acted uniformly and as a matter of inner conviction: “My daily secretiveness and the secret of my internal life don’t allow me to become a person with an independent character. I can’t come out openly or sharply, with any free thoughts. Instead I have to say only what everybody says . . . Unwittingly I’m acquiring the character of a toady, of a cunning dog: soft, cowardly, and always giving in. How trite and how disgusting!”

Podlubny’s work for the GPU was not entirely a matter of concealment and adaptation. The reports he wrote on the “moods” of the young workers in the Pravda plant evolved from observations that pre-dated his recruitment as an informant. His diary of 1932 repeatedly mentions a certain member of his brigade, a worker named Anisin. In May Anisin caused a scandal by typesetting a counterrevolutionary slogan. While the Komsomol investigated Anisin’s background, Podlubny received a reprimand as brigade leader. Later that year Anisin, who also attended the literary circle, read sections from his diary to Podlubny. Interpreting the passages as direct expressions of Anisin’s character, Podlubny was appalled: “How opposite our writings are. He’s such an egoist. Amazing. He wants to be a person who looks upon his environment with indifference. That’s deadly boring. True, he’s an indeterminate sort of person, and, true, it’s hard to say what sort of fellow he is, you can’t figure out what his ideas are.” In November the GPU assigned Podlubny to observe Anisin, who had meanwhile been expelled from the Komsomol. Podlubny’s report is not available, but in his diary he characterized Anisin’s behavior as “suspicious and deceitful,” seamlessly elaborating on his earlier views of his “indeterminate” co-worker.

“Counterrevolutionary” moods were widespread among young workers in the plant, Podlubny noted in his diary. He called upon the GPU to step in and intensify its “educational work.” He cast the secret police as a moral authority, whose vocation was to correct the consciousness of erring individuals and thus restore their shattered psychological health. Podlubny also supported the GPU’s concern for social hygiene. He once reported to his contact officer that he had been approached in a park by a man who wanted to have sex with him. Podlubny provided the man’s name, which he had made a point of obtaining. The GPU showed interest in the case and told him that the suspect would be “unmasked” shortly. Podlubny’s reports were not confined to the moral health of Soviet youth.

在他的文件中保存着一份对他的工头扎哈罗夫的举报，扎哈罗夫是在他学徒期间骚扰过他的教官。波德卢布内谴责扎哈罗夫是一个根深蒂固的“反动分子”，他只谈论苏联生活的缺点，却不提及其成就。此外，他指控扎哈罗夫试图将他的“旧观念”强加给学徒们，其中一些人受其影响，开始表现出“消极”和“落后”的态度。总而言之，这些报告表明格别乌对苏联社会的政治分类与波德卢布内对自己及其社会环境的私人看法之间存在相当大的重叠和互动。波德卢布内为格别乌撰写的报告，以其对年轻人不健康、不良、消极、反动观点的鲜明强调，读起来就像是他日记中自我改造工作的延伸，他在日记中试图摆脱自己的“黑色思想”。

Preserved among his papers is a denunciation of his foreman at work, Zakharov, the instructor who had harassed him during his apprenticeship. Podlubny denounced Zakharov as an inveterate “reactionary” who talked only about the shortcomings of Soviet life while failing to mention its achievements. Moreover, he charged Zakharov with seeking to impose his “old views” on the apprentices, some of whom had fallen under his sway and begun to exhibit “passive” and “backward” attitudes. Taken as a whole, these reports demonstrate a considerable degree of overlap and interaction between the GPU’s political taxonomy of Soviet society and Podlubny’s private views of himself and his social environment. With their stark emphases on unhealthy, bad, passive, reactionary views of youth, Podlubny’s reports for the GPU read like an extension of the work of self-transformation in the diary, in which he sought to rid himself of his own black thoughts.

波德卢布内被格别乌招募后不久，他和他的母亲又面临了一个严峻的挑战。1932年12月下旬的一项政府法令宣布，所有城市居民都必须办理内部护照。通过强制个人向市政府登记，苏联政府试图对农民涌入城市施加一定程度的控制。由于集体化导致的农业危机，以及饥荒蔓延农村的最初迹象，农民以前所未有的数量离开村庄，威胁到城市配给系统的资源超负荷。但护照法也被引入，以清除城市中的阶级异己，并将没有获得护照的农民束缚到新建的集体农庄。
由格别乌和莫斯科刑警组成的核查委员会，逐栋楼房进行检查，核查证件并没收被剥夺选举权者以及从集体农场逃离的农民的文件。仅在波德卢布内居住的楼房里，警察就没收了四十张口粮卡，并命令其持有者立即离开城市。波德卢布内一家已经以防万一地打包好了行李，但他们被允许保留他们的口粮卡，大概是因为他们伪造文件的可信度，以及他们两人都在莫斯科有工作。然而，和所有人一样，他们不得不等待，看他们是否会获得护照。

在他的日记中，波德卢布内努力辨别护照运动的目的。对他来说，挑战在于发现国家利益，以便顺应它并因此得救。当他第一次听说新护照时，记录的一则初始日记表达了迷茫：“我该怎么活？！该怎么办？！！我会在哪里看到自己的影子？我该怎—么—做……？我看起来怎么样！！！为什么没有关于这方面的任何东西可读！？”后来，在核查委员会检查过他所在的楼房，并且他听说了其他人对护照运动的看法后，波德卢布内认为他理解了其原理。这场清洗是一项社会卫生措施，“一台最新型的人类清洗机器。被需要的人通过筛子，而那些有着富有过去的人则作为废料留下。”国家着手“筛选”并清除那些它不需要用于社会主义建设的社会元素。这场清洗的目标群体包括“投机者”、“酒鬼”和“小偷”，以及被剥夺选举权的人，以及通常是那些“有着富有过去”的人。这些人与众不同之处在于他们被污染的心理，这使他们无法从事有益于社会的工作。他将这个群体与模范的“诚实公民”对立起来：勤恳工作，致力于国家利益。波德卢布内希望新护照能在国家和公民之间建立一个契约，一个坚定的社会契约，要求每个人更努力地工作，反过来又给予明确的利益：不仅是口粮卡和工资，更重要的是，成为苏联国家“家庭”的一员，从而获得布尔什维克政权认可的不可侵犯的自我感。
但日记也显示，这种由有益工作定义的主体性，在无休止地搜寻隐藏敌人的过程中是多么不稳定。一名与波德卢布内共事的年轻女子在被揭露为商人女儿并被威胁驱逐出莫斯科后，试图用灭鼠药自杀。

Shortly after Podlubny was recruited by the GPU, he and his mother faced another formidable challenge. A government decree of late December 1932 announced the introduction of passports for all urban citizens. By making it mandatory for individuals to register with the city administration, the Soviet government sought to assume a degree of control over peasant in-migration to the cities. With the agricultural crisis induced by collectivization, and with the first indications of a famine spreading over the countryside, peasants left the villages in unprecedented numbers, threatening to exceed the resources of the rationing system in the cities. But the passport law was also introduced to purge the cities of class aliens and chain the peasants, who did not receive passports, to the newly established kolkhozes.

Verification commissions, staffed by the GPU and the Moscow criminal police, went from building to building, checking papers and confiscating documents from disenfranchised persons as well as from peasants who had fled from collective farms. Police agents confiscated forty ration cards in Podlubny’s building alone and ordered their owners to leave the city immediately. The Podlubnys had already packed up just in case, but they were allowed to keep their ration cards, presumably because of the plausibility of their forged documents and because they both had employment in Moscow. Like everyone else, however, they had to wait and see whether they would receive passports.

In his diary Podlubny struggled to identify the purpose of the passport campaign. The challenge for him was to discover the state interest in order to conform to it and thus be saved. An initial entry, recorded when he first heard about the new passports, expressed disorientation: “How am I supposed to live?! What is to be done?!! Where will I see the mirror of myself? How should I beha-a-a-a-ve . . . ? How do I look!!! Why is there nothing to read on this!?” Later, after the verification commission had come through his building and he had heard what other people were saying about the passport campaign, Podlubny believed he understood its rationale. The purge was a social hygiene measure, “a machine for human cleansing of the newest type. Those who are needed pass through the sieve, and as waste remain the people with a wealthy past.” The state proceeded to “sift out” and discard those elements of society which it did not need for the ongoing construction of socialism. The groups targeted by the purge included “speculators,” “alcoholics,” and “thieves” as well as disenfranchised people and, generally, those “with a wealthy past.” What distinguished these people was their tainted psychology, which made them incapable of performing socially useful work. To this group he opposed the exemplary “honest citizen”: earnest and hardworking, dedicated to the interests of the state. Podlubny hoped that the new passports would create a contract between state and citizen, a firm social contract requiring each individual to work harder but in turn granting distinct benefits: not only a ration card and a salary but, more important, membership in the “family” of the Soviet state and thus an inviolable sense of self, sanctioned by the Bolshevik regime.

But the diary also shows how unstable this subjectivity defined by useful work remained in the face of an unending search for hidden enemies. A young woman who worked with Podlubny tried to kill herself with rat poison after she had been unmasked as the daughter of a tradesman and threatened with expulsion from Moscow.
工厂里一名党的官员在讲话中阐述了护照运动的目标：50%的学徒将被清洗。波德卢布内猜测，莫斯科市民中同样比例的人口将被驱逐。

这些事件促使波德卢布内修改了他的自我定义。他确信自己无法通过这场人类清洗机器，他称自己为“杂草”，将被筛选过程从“被选中的种子”中剔除。在同一则日记中，他提到他和母亲改变了他们的“适应策略”。这是有道理的，因为如果他知道自己与新秩序格格不入，那么唯一能存活下来的方法就是欺骗政权。他的策略是成为一个取悦当局的“谄媚者”；他母亲的策略是成为一名优秀学生。然而，他仍然担心他们注定要失败：“我们正走向灾难。按照计算，95个会失败，只有5个会成功。”
当他感觉到国家愿意恢复前阶级异己的权利时，波德卢布内认为自己是一名优秀且忠诚的苏联工人。然而，一旦融合似乎被拒绝，他便将自己定义为一个非苏联分子，一颗只有通过狡猾或偶然才能在良好的社会主义土壤中生长的坏种子。

A party official speaking in the plant formulated the goal of the passport campaign: 50 percent of all apprentices were to be purged. Podlubny guessed that the same percentage of Moscow’s citizens would be deported.

These events prompted Podlubny to modify his self-definition. Convinced that he would not make it through the human cleansing machine, he referred to himself as “weed” that the sifting process would discard from the “chosen seeds.” In the same entry he mentioned that he and his mother had changed their “tactics of adaptation.” This made sense, for if he knew himself to be alien to the new order, the only way to prevail was to deceive the regime. His tactic was to become a “toady” who pleased the authorities; his mother’s was to be an excellent student. Still, he feared they were doomed: “We’re headed for disaster. With a calculation of 95 lost and only 5 will win.”

When he sensed that the state was willing to rehabilitate former class aliens, Podlubny considered himself a good and committed Soviet worker. Yet as soon as integration appeared to be withheld, he defined himself as a non-Soviet element, a bad seed that could make it onto good socialist soil only by way of cunning or chance.
1933年4月，波德卢布内和他的母亲收到了他们的新护照。这似乎巩固了他们作为国家所选良善工人的身份。几周后写的一则欣喜若狂的日记中，波德卢布内不再将苏联制度描绘成他必须与之抗争或适应的东西，因为他已成为其中的有机组成部分。他自己的利益与国家的利益融合在了一起：
最近我开始将我的社会工作视为一种生活方式，而不是谋取个人前程的手段，视为我身体和存在的一部分，如同生存不可或缺的面包，而非争夺生存的斗争，而是一个我乐意接受的体系。而且，这种对我的身心来说不可或缺的规律性一天比一天更强、更牢固。我已经明显地改造了自己，不再一心谋求个人前程，而是把工作当成像食物一样必需的生活方式，我毫不费力地投入时间。这很好。我为此感到高兴。

In April 1933 Podlubny and his mother received their new passports. This seemed to cement their identities as good workers chosen by the state. In a euphoric entry written several weeks later, Podlubny no longer portrayed the Soviet system as something he had to fight or adapt to, since he had become an organic part of it. His own interests and the interests of the state had fused:

Lately I’ve come to view my social work not as careerism but as a system, as a component part of my body and my existence, as the bread that is indispensable in order to exist, not a struggle for existence but a system that I willingly embrace. And with every day this constancy, this system, which is necessary for my organism, becomes stronger, becomes more firmly established. I have noticeably reeducated myself from careerism to a system that is necessary like food, to which I devote my time without any effort. That’s good. I’m happy about it.
然而，随着时间的推移，熟悉的不确定性重新浮现。无论是工作场所、共青团，还是在格别乌（GPU）办公室，警惕的气氛都没有减弱，随时都可能瓦解波德卢布内为自己建立的结构。他身份悬而未决的问题，在其1934年新日记的扉页上得到了醒目的表达。该扉页采用构成主义风格，印有一个巨大的红色问号和一行题词：“你又像一条蟒蛇一样悬在我头顶。”
波德卢布内大约在同一时间创作的一首诗，描绘了他公开暴露身份的噩梦般景象。他最担心的是被排斥，是被排除在那个以集体和社会用途为尺度的世界之外、孤独生活的前景：

Over time, however, the familiar uncertainties resurfaced. The atmosphere of vigilance, whether at the workplace, in the Komsomol, or in the GPU offices, did not diminish, and it threatened to undo at any moment the structure that Podlubny had built for himself. The unresolved question of his identity was glaringly expressed on the cover page of his new diary for 1934. Executed in constructivist style, it featured a huge red question mark and the caption “Again you hang above me like a boa [constrictor].”

A poem Podlubny composed around the same time imagined the nightmarish vision of his public unmasking. What he feared most was ostracism, the prospect of a lonely existence outside and beyond a world he measured in terms of collectivities and usefulness to society:

今天——办公室
人们会在那里对我提出质疑
我被恐惧攫住
也许我会回来
不再是波德卢布内，
一个讨人喜欢的人
大家信赖的人
但会走出
被所有人熟知
令所有人感到恐惧
无人需要，
完全孤单。

Today—the office
And questions will be raised about me there
I’m gripped by fear
Perhaps I will return
No longer Podlubny,
A pleasant fellow
And authority for everyone
But will walk out
Known everywhere
Terrifying to everyone
Needed by no one,
Completely alone.
波德卢布内知道，他的“游戏”迟早会因其出身被发现而结束。最迟，这必须在他学徒期结束时参加兵役征召时发生。必要的背景调查将会揭露他赖以生存的欺骗。

Sooner or later, Podlubny knew, his “game” would end with the discovery of his origins. At the very latest, this had to happen when he came up for the military draft at the end of his apprenticeship. The required background check would bring to light the deceit on which his  life was built.

1934年10月，他一直担心的事件发生了。他正在与他的秘密警察联络员进行例行会议，联络员的主管也在场。“他们完全出乎意料地问了我这些可怕的问题。我不知道为什么，但我并没有真正失去镇静。我脸红了，没有回答，只是仔细听着。他们没有问太多问题。如果我理解正确的话，他们主要是对我为什么隐瞒他们感到不满。整个谈话持续了不到十分钟……我们谈得很开放，也很冷静。”

波德卢布内没有失去冷静的一个原因是，就在几天前，苏联报纸刊登了法令，准许那些能够证明自己为苏联国家真诚工作了五年的富农和其他阶级异己分子恢复公民身份。鉴于这项新立法，波德卢布内认为他身份暴露的后果不会太严重。至少他期望国家能给他明确的行为准则。因此，他将自己的身份暴露视为一个“历史时刻”，是他“非法”生活的终结。但他的内务人民委员部（NKVD）联络员告诉他（国家政治保卫局格别乌已于1934年夏天改名为内务人民委员部
），只要他继续为他们好好工作，就不会受到惩罚。

In October 1934 the event he had been dreading took place. He was at a regular meeting with his secret police contact officer, in the presence of the officer’s supervisor. “Totally unexpectedly they asked me these terrible questions. I don’t know why, but I didn’t really lose my composure. Blushed, didn’t answer, just listened carefully. They didn’t ask many questions. If I understood it correctly, they were mainly upset about why I had concealed it from them. The whole conversation didn’t last more than ten minutes . . . We talked very openly and coolly.”

One reason Podlubny did not lose his cool was that just days earlier Soviet newspapers had published decrees granting civic rehabilitation to kulaks and other class aliens who could demonstrate that they had worked sincerely for the Soviet state for five years. In light of this new legislation Podlubny thought the repercussions of his unmasking would not be too serious. At the very least he expected the state to give him clear guidelines on how to behave. Thus he hailed his un-masking as a “historical moment,” the end of his “illegal” life. But all that his NKVD contact officers told him (the GPU had been renamed the NKVD in the summer of 1934) was that he would not be punished as long as he continued to do good work for them.
1935年春天，波德卢布内的一位同事被揭露是富农的儿子。令人惊讶的是，他没有发生任何事情。对波德卢布内来说，这表明国家正在改变其对阶级异己分子的政策。重要的不再是一个人的过去，而是他当前的工作表现。他再次相信自己正在见证一个“历史时刻”：
也许从现在开始，我的新世界观将开始形成。我被接纳为苏联大家庭的一员，和其他所有人一样，这一想法促使我以爱回报那些促成此事的人。我不再与我一直恐惧的敌人在一起，无论何时何地，无论我在哪里。我不再害怕我的环境。我与其他人一样，因此我应该对各种事物感兴趣，就像农场主对自己的农场感兴趣一样，而不是像农场工人对待他的主人那样。
波德卢布内一次又一次地表达了这样的期望：一旦他在苏联社会获得合法地位，他将从根本上得到转变。他认为自己的非法地位是他所有问题的根源。这迫使他将自己的环境视为充满敌意。他可以适应其生活形式，但无法有机地融入其中。跨过合法化的门槛，波德卢布内期望发现一种新的、非强制的、对国家的完全奉献——爱。与此同时，他将摆脱根深蒂固的心理，成为苏维埃家庭的一员，并获得与社会主义“人格”相称的完整世界观。

In the spring of 1935 a colleague of Podlubny’s was exposed as the son of a kulak. Surprisingly, nothing happened to him. To Podlubny this indicated that the state was changing its policy toward class aliens. What mattered was no longer one’s past but one’s current work performance. Once more he believed he was witnessing a “historical moment”:

Perhaps from here on my new worldview will begin to emerge. The thought that I’ve been made a citizen of the common family of the USSR like everybody else obliges me to respond with love to those who have done this. I am no longer with the enemy, whom I fear all the time, every moment, wherever I am. I no longer fear my environment. I am just like everybody else, and therefore I should be interested in various things, just the way a master is interested in his farm, and not like a farm laborer toward his master.

Time and again Podlubny voiced the expectation that he would be fundamentally transformed as soon as he received legal standing in Soviet society. He saw his illegal standing as the source of his problems. It forced him to view his environment as hostile. He could adapt to its forms of life, but he could not organically merge with them. In crossing the threshold of legalization, Podlubny expected to discover a new sense of uncoerced and total devotion to the state—love. At the same time he would outgrow his ingrained psychology, become a member of the Soviet family, and acquire an integrated worldview befitting the socialist “personality.”
1935年秋，波德卢布内被莫斯科第二医学院录取。多年来，他一直梦想成为一名学生，但他的社会出身似乎阻碍了这一梦想的实现。每位大学入学候选人的履历都受到严格审查，波德卢布内不得不担心当局会发现他的富农背景。然而，凭借共青团和《真理报》工厂的推荐，他被学院录取了。从表面上看，他现在符合社会主义新人的理想。医学专业生涯似乎触手可及。

In the fall of 1935 Podlubny was accepted into Moscow’s Second Medical Institute. For years he had dreamed of becoming a student, but his social origins had seemed to prevent the fulfillment of this dream. The biography of each candidate for admission to a university was thoroughly scrutinized, and Podlubny had to fear that the authorities would discover his kulak past. Yet, with recommendations from the Komsomol and the Pravda plant, he was admitted to the institute. On the face of it, he now conformed to the ideal of a socialist new man. A professional career in medicine seemed to be within his reach.

children: 波德卢布内对转变的追求，在很大程度上决定了他建立和断绝的人际关系。他对新生活形式的渴望，与他希望获得的改良“心理”相符，影响了他与莫斯科的朋友和同事以及他乌克兰故乡的熟人的交往，并极大地干预了他的个人和家庭生活。首先，它重新定义了他与父亲菲利普·叶夫多基莫维奇的关系。斯捷潘童年的记忆，在日记的不同地方勾勒出来，描绘了一个动辄惩罚独子的施虐父亲。在父亲在“去富农化”运动中被判行政流放后，斯捷潘与这位“暴君”分离时，他经历了一个解放的时刻。那是他生命中的一个转折点：只有在那时他才开始获得意识并“成长”。这当然是一个回顾性的叙述，是在他父亲被捕近三年后写成的。
斯捷潘当时是否这样想过他的父亲不得而知。斯捷潘和他的母亲选择前往流放地与菲利普团聚的事实表明并非如此。但斯捷潘在斯大林统治下的俄罗斯将自己定义为一名城市公民，这要求他以如此鲜明的措辞来否定他的旧生活，而他的父亲就是这种旧生活的缩影。

Podlubny’s quest for transformation determined in great measure the relationships he forged, as well as those he severed. His desire for a new form of life, in tune with the reformed “psychology” he hoped to acquire, affected his interactions with friends and colleagues in Moscow, as well as with acquaintances from his former home in Ukraine, and it dramatically cut into his personal and family life. In the first instance it redefined his relationship with his father, Filip Evdokimovich. Stepan’s memories of his childhood, sketched out in various places in the diary, evoke an abusive father who punished his only son at every step. Stepan experienced a moment of liberation when he was separated from the “tyrant” after his father was sentenced to administrative exile during the dekulakization campaign. That was a turning point in his life: only then did he start to gain consciousness and “grow.” This, to be sure, was a retrospective account, written nearly three years after his father’s arrest.

Whether Stepan had thought about his father this way at the time is unknown. The fact that Stepan and his mother chose to join Filip in his exile suggests otherwise. But Stepan’s self-definition as an urban citizen in Stalin’s Russia called for a repudiation of his old life, epitomized by his father, in such stark terms.

菲利普·叶夫多基莫维奇在完成三年的流放期后，于1933年4月在莫斯科与家人团聚。他找到了一份装卸工的工作，并获得了临时居住证。尽管地位不稳，他在莫斯科的身份是合法的，但他与妻子和儿子同住的事实有可能暴露他们隐瞒的社会背景。斯捷潘指责父亲的鲁莽行为使家人陷入危险。然而，更让他不安的是父亲没有改掉的旧习气。尽管在流放中有机会重塑自我，但他依然“老旧”、“落后”和“无用”。斯捷潘将他父亲描绘成一个“无用的老人”，并非因为他的生理年龄（他当时45岁），而是因为他没有努力成为一个对社会有用的苏联公民。在整个日记中，斯捷潘强调了他与父亲在情感和智力上的疏离。他称他为“生父，但教育上的陌生人”或干脆是他的“前任父亲”，以此突出血缘关系与通过意识所建立的关系之间的对比。意识纽带超越了亲缘关系，从而证明了斯捷潘尽管与旧秩序有血缘关系，但仍要求被承认为新秩序一员的权利。

Filip Evdokimovich was reunited with the family in Moscow in April 1933, upon completion of his three-year term of exile. He found work as a loader and obtained a temporary residence permit. While precarious, his standing in Moscow was legal, but the fact that he lived with his wife and son threatened to betray their concealed social background. Stepan blamed his father’s imprudence for putting the family in danger. He was even more upset, however, by his father’s unreformed ways. Despite the opportunity to remake himself in exile, he had remained “old,” “backward,” and “useless.” Stepan portrayed his father as a “useless old man,” not because of his biological age (he was 45), but because he made no effort to become a socially useful Soviet citizen. Throughout the diary Stepan emphasized his emotional and intellectual detachment from his father. Calling him a “father by conception but a stranger by education” or simply his “former father,” he made a point of contrasting relationships based on blood to those forged by consciousness. Bonds of consciousness superseded those of kinship and thus justified Stepan’s claim to be recognized as a member of the new order in spite of his blood ties to the old.

波德卢布内对他与父亲关系的描述，不仅仅可以被解释为一个青少年争取身份认同的挣扎：他选择的概念和强调点可以从历史角度看作是更大文化文本的一部分。波德卢布内将他与父亲之间的对立，用苏联工业化斗争的核心术语来表达：社会中“旧”与“新”元素、“落后”与“进步”、黑暗与光明之间的斗争。他对他父亲的指责都围绕着成长、自我改变和为社会服务这些核心革命要求。他的父亲不仅未能“自我完善”，未能培养出坚强的品格，而且未能证明他对社会的有用性。此外，过去他曾试图通过不让儿子上学、让他去放羊来阻碍他的“成长”。

Podlubny’s account of his relationship with his father can be inter-preted as more than just an adolescent’s struggle for identity: the concepts and emphases he selected can be situated historically as part of a larger cultural text. Podlubny couched the opposition between himself and his father in terms that were central to the battle for Soviet industrialization: a struggle between “old” and “new” elements in society, “backward” and “progressive,” darkness and light. His reproaches of his father all revolved around the central revolutionary mandates of growth, self-change, and service to society. Not only did his father fail to “work on himself,” develop into a strong character, but he failed to demonstrate his usefulness to society. Moreover, in the past he had tried to stem his son’s “growth” by keeping him out of school to tend the goats.

然而，尽管斯捷潘用布尔什维克的革命语言谴责他的父亲，但他并没有以一个坚定的布尔什维克所应有的方式与父亲对峙。党号召青年，特别是那些出身有问题的人，与他们的父亲划清界限，并将他们谴责为阶级敌人。阶级异己出身的子女发表的仪式性声明充斥着地方和国家报纸，他们否定自己的父母，并宣称已与他们断绝一切联系。在这些儿子中，有著名的帕夫利克·莫罗佐夫，他据称向当局举报了他的富农父亲，随后被他的叔叔杀害。帕夫利克被宣布为烈士，成为苏联青年效仿的榜样。

斯捷潘·波德卢布内远远没有做出这种行为。即使在他的日记中，他也没有将父亲诋毁为“富农”或敌人；更不用说考虑公开谴责他了。即便如此，他对“老人”的敌意也足够真实。日记记录了父子之间因菲利普酒后与妻子争吵而引发的口角，这表明了农民的父权世界是如何崩塌的，以及共产主义的节制、纪律和个人自尊价值观作为赋权和道德权威的来源，对农民家属有多大的吸引力。菲利普在1933年只与家人住了几个月。那年夏天，他和叶夫罗西尼娅拜访了他们的乌克兰故乡，他希望能在那重新定居。他们被地方当局赶走了。回到莫斯科后，菲利普搬到了他自己的住处。

And yet, while Stepan condemned his father in the revolutionary language of Bolshevism, he did not confront him in ways that befitted a committed Bolshevik. The party appealed to youth, especially to those with tainted backgrounds, to dissociate themselves from their fathers and denounce them as class enemies. Ritualistic declarations by sons and daughters of class-alien heritage filled the local and national press, repudiating their parents and stating that they had severed all ties to them. Among these sons was the famous Pavlik Morozov, who allegedly reported his kulak father to the authorities and was then killed by his uncle. Pavlik was declared a martyr and a model to be emulated by Soviet youth.

Stepan Podlubny stopped well short of such behavior. Not even in his diary did he vilify his father as a “kulak” or an enemy; much less did he entertain the thought of denouncing him publicly. Even so, his hostility toward the “old man” was real enough. The diary records altercations between father and son, provoked by Filip’s drunken fights with his wife, that suggest how the patriarchal world of the peasantry had come tumbling down, and how much the Communist values of sobriety, discipline, and individual self-respect appealed to peasants’ dependents as sources of empowerment and moral authority. Filip stayed with his family for only a few months in 1933. That summer he and Yefrosinia visited their Ukrainian home village, where he hoped to resettle. They were chased away by the local authorities. After they returned to Moscow, Filip moved to a place of his own.
斯捷潘非常敬佩他的母亲。他赞扬她逐渐表现出的“无产阶级观点”，暗示她也像他一样，接受了改造自己的必要性。他的母亲上夜校，并从事出色的社会工作，为此她获得了奖项。斯捷潘的日记引用了他母亲从一个夏季劳动营写给他的信，她被派去那里割泥炭：“收到了妈妈的信。我非常高兴她在她的‘移民’过程中得到了一点再教育。她写道，尽管工作非常困难，‘我将待满整个月直到胜利结束。’这非常好。这是无产阶级的方式。”
在与人交往中，波德卢布内竭力将自己塑造成一个进步和“有教养”价值观的承载者。他坚决拒绝带有原始主义和乡村“落后”色彩的语言或态度。他所在的那栋楼位于红色无产阶级街，其中一个侧翼被罗丁一家占用，他们是来自卡卢加省的农民移民。斯捷潘称他们的公寓为“罗丁村”，因为这家人为所有来到莫斯科找工作的亲戚和熟人提供了临时住所。

斯捷潘和他的母亲刚到这座城市时，也曾住在罗丁家。这间公寓也是年轻人聚会的地点，斯捷潘有时会去那里聊天和玩乐。然而，他始终将“罗丁村”描绘成农民落后和野蛮的堡垒：“年轻人聚集在罗丁家厨房里唱歌跳舞。这些年轻人都是村里的——来自一个落后、极其低层的环境的男孩和女孩。你站在那里看着他们，乍一看是一幅令人愉悦的画面。但当你更仔细地思考时，你会退缩，因为你记得这些人是活生生的人。人！不是动物。但他们彼此间的关系、思想和举止就像动物一样。”

Stepan greatly admired his mother. He praised her for the “proletarian views” she had gradually come to exhibit, implying that, like him, she had accepted the need to rework herself. His mother attended evening school and performed outstanding social work for which she received awards. Stepan’s diary cites a letter she wrote to him from a summer work camp where she had been sent to cut peat: “Received a letter from Mama. Am very happy that she has reeducated herself a little in the course of her ‘emigration.’ She writes that, in spite of the great difficulty of the work, ‘I’ll stay for the entire month until the victorious end.’ This is very good. This is the proletarian way.”

In his interactions with people Podlubny was at pains to represent himself as a bearer of progressive and “cultured” values. He emphatically rejected language or attitudes that smacked of primitivism and village “backwardness.” A wing of his building on Red Proletarian Street was occupied by the Rodin family, peasant in-migrants from Kaluga province. Stepan called their apartment the “Rodin village,” because the family gave temporary shelter to all their relatives and acquaintances who came to Moscow in search of work.

Stepan and his mother, too, had stayed with the Rodins when they first arrived in the city. The apartment was also a meeting point for youth, and Stepan went there on occasion to chat and have a good time. Nevertheless, he consistently portrayed the “Rodin village” as a bulwark of peasant backwardness and barbarism: “The young people come together to dance and sing in the Rodins’ kitchen. These young people are all from the village—girls and boys from a backward, extremely low milieu. You stand there and look at them, a pleasant picture at first sight. But when you think about it more carefully, you draw back, because you remember that these are living people. People! Not animals. But their relations with one another, their thoughts and manners are just animal-like.”

这一醉酒场景为波德卢布内提供了一个对比，他借此确立了自己作为新人的感觉。他详细描述了他与其他学徒的活动，他们都努力追求教育、道德自我完善和得体的穿着。这些是区分“有文化”青年的追求：“今天我们三个人，科利亚·加兰金、费德卡·康德拉季耶夫和我，在剧院度过了一个有文化且非常美好的夜晚。内心充满了令人愉悦的感觉。它让我想起了某种宏伟、成熟而又新颖的事物。这与花一卢布去街角看电影不同。不，去剧院，这是一件严肃、有文化的事情，而且要花五卢布。你支付多少钱具有巨大的道德意义。”
斯捷潘·波德卢布内1936年拍摄的一张肖像照，象征着有文化人的理想。照片中，他身穿时髦西装，手放在一张帝国风格的矮沙发上，在摄影工作室里摆姿势。背景中厚重的窗帘，展现了斯大林主义文化的新古典主义抱负。拍摄这张肖像照需要波德卢布内付出象征性和物质上的投资；这表明他重视将自己表现为社会主义时代一个发展成熟的个体。

This drunken scene supplied Podlubny with a contrast against which he could establish his sense of himself as a new man. In as much detail he described his activities with other apprentices who shared his striving toward education, moral self-improvement, and proper attire. These were the pursuits that distinguished “cultured” youth: “Today the three of us, Kolya Galankin, Fyedka Kondratyev, and I, spent a cultured and very good evening at the theater. Remarkably pleasant feelings of the heart. It reminded me of something grandiose, adult, and new at the same time. It’s not the same as going to the movies around the corner for a ruble. No, to the theater, a serious, cultured matter, and for five rubles. It has a huge moral significance, how much you pay.”

A portrait of Stepan Podlubny, taken in 1936, emblematizes the ideal of the cultured person. It shows him posing in a photographer’s studio, wearing a fashionable suit, his hand resting on an Empire-style banquette. The setting, with heavy curtains in the background, illustrates the neoclassical aspirations of Stalinist culture. Having his portrait taken required an investment, symbolic and material, on Podlubny’s part; it bespeaks the importance he attached to representing himself as a developed individual of the socialist age.
另一个社会地位提升的时刻，在字面意义上也是向上的，发生在1935年，当时波德卢布内一家终于逃离了他们潮湿的地下室房间。他们那栋楼二楼的一个政府办公室空了出来，在随后的准租户争夺战中，母子俩设法为自己争取到了半间房和两扇窗户。另一名租户住在同一个房间里，隔着一个临时屏风。那套公寓由十三个家庭共同居住。

Another moment of upward mobility, in a quite literal sense, took place in 1935, when the Podlubnys managed to escape from their humid basement room. A government office had been vacated on the second floor of their building, and in the ensuing battle among would-be tenants, mother and son managed to claim half a room and two windows for themselves. Another tenant lived in the same room, behind a makeshift screen. The apartment was shared by thirteen families.

在寻求受过教育且举止优雅的青年为伴时，斯捷潘有些担忧地注意到，在找女朋友方面，他似乎在“没文化”的“最底层阶级”中表现得最好。有一段时间他曾和一个名叫塔尼娅的女孩约会，他喜欢她的长相，也喜欢她对他真挚的爱。但他担心，如果他继续和她在一起，这标志着他也属于最底层阶级，属于心理和智力低人一等的一类人。仿佛为了反驳这种怀疑，他给她写了长篇大论、内容散漫的信，其中一封长达14页，讲述他对她矛盾的感情，尽管他知道她文化程度不高，读不懂也理解不了。他的长信实际上是写给她的那些更“成熟”的女友的，斯捷潘确信她们会读给塔尼娅听并解释给她听。当他收到塔尼娅的回信时，他失声大笑。那短短几行字是按发音书写的，几乎每个单词都有拼写错误。这封信证实了他的感觉：塔尼娅和他在约会的其他女孩一样，仅仅是“炮灰”，不可能成为他的长期女友或妻子。他很快断绝了关系，在另一封信中解释说，他被她的“真诚”和“忠诚”所感动，但她“完全文盲”和表达的“粗鲁”让他无法接受。
一篇日记记录了波德卢布内认为自己悬浮其间的两个截然不同的“环境”。一个由塔尼娅定义，另一个由大学生波琳娜定义：

While seeking the company of educated and refined youth, Stepan noted with some concern that when it came to girlfriends he seemed to do best with “uncultured” types, “from the lowest class.” For a while he  dated a girl named Tanya, whom he liked for her looks and her sincere love for him. But he feared that if he remained with her, this would signify that he, too, was from the lowest class, a psychologically and intellectually inferior type of person. As if to counter this suspicion, he wrote her rambling letters, one of them fourteen pages long, about his contradictory feelings toward her, even though he knew she was not literate enough to read and understand them. His long letter in fact was addressed to her more “developed” girlfriends, who, Stepan was certain, would read and explain it to Tanya. When he received Tanya’s reply, he burst out laughing. The few lines were written phonetically, with spelling mistakes in almost every word. The letter confirmed his feeling that Tanya, like other girls he had dated, was mere “cannon fodder” and could not possibly become his steady girlfriend or his wife. He quickly broke off the relationship, explaining in another letter that he felt touched by her “sincerity” and “loyalty,” but that her “complete illiteracy” and the “crudeness” of her expression had turned him off.
